rgb: This indoor lounge has large windows lining the left wall with trees visible outside. An unoccupied grey armchair holding two pillows stands approximately 2 to 2.5 metres ahead of the camera wearer, with a floor lamp directly to the chair’s right. A second person is seated immediately to the camera wearer’s right, about 0.5 to 0.8 metres away; their torso, hands, smartphone, and green lanyard appear in the lower-right foreground, while the edge of their face and glasses is partly cut off at the upper-right corner in the early frames. The nearby person faces toward the left side of the frame, angled downward at the smartphone held in both hands, and watches its screen instead of looking at the camera wearer. The phone, their hands, the armrest separating the two people, and the closest corner of a low glass table at the bottom left—roughly 0.8 to 1 metre away—are within or barely at the boundary of the camera wearer’s reach, although the phone remains directly in the other person’s hands. Against the left wall, around 2.5 metres away, are a small dark shelf and a white side table. Farther away, 5 to 7 metres into the upper-right background, sit another armchair and a windowed alcove with a desk and chair, partly blocked by the foreground lamp pole and an interior wall pillar. Neither person moves during the five frames. In frame 3, the camera wearer’s view tilts slightly upward and left, briefly pushing more of the nearby person’s head and the glass table outside the image, before angling slightly downward and right again in frames 4 and 5.
depth: The depth visualization depicts the indoor lounge in several distance layers. On the immediate right, a seated person appears bright white at about 0.4–0.7 m away and holds a smartphone with both hands, placing it within both their reach and the camera wearer’s reach. Ahead in the middle distance is an empty armchair with two throw pillows at roughly 1.8–2.5 m, approximately 1.5 m beyond the seated person. A floor-lamp pole and another chair armrest occupy the space between them at around 1.0–2.2 m, while the left-side window wall lies about 2.5–3.5 m away and opens toward a deeper room in the upper-right background at more than 4 m. Cropped heavily by the right and bottom borders, the person faces left in profile and looks toward the phone instead of the camera wearer. In frames 3 and 4, they move slightly backward or beyond the upper-right edge as the camera tilts a little downward and left, then reappear in frame 5. Their arms and phone partly block the foreground chair armrest and the central armchair’s lower-right corner, while that middle-ground armchair and the lamp pole partially hide the background room. Relative to the RGB sequence, the depth view distinctly divides the nearby person, intermediate chair armrest, middle-ground armchair, and narrow vertical lamp pole into separate depth layers. Its estimates are unreliable for the outdoor trees visible through the left windows, however, flattening them to the same indoor depth of about 3 m as the window wall. It also merges the armchair’s thin dark metal legs and the foreground glass tabletop into the floor’s depth gradient.
segmentation: The segmentation output separates the central armchair—marked yellow as ‘couch’ and located about 1.8–2.5 m ahead—the lower-right foreground chair armrest, classified as ‘chair’ at approximately 1.0–1.2 m, the small plant on the left windowsill around 2.8 m away and about 1.5 m left of the armchair, and a far armchair in the rear-right room labelled ‘couch’ or ‘bed’ at roughly 4.5–5.5 m. It also inconsistently segments the seated person at the bottom right with a tan/brown mask in frames 1, 2, and 4, at about 0.4–0.7 m, as well as the smartphone held between their hands with a grey mask in frame 4 at approximately 0.6 m. These masks reveal that the foreground person and armrest overlap the central armchair’s lower-right corner. Through the 5 frames, minor head tilting by the camera wearer causes the masks to move slightly both horizontally and vertically. When the camera turns a little left in frames 3 and 4, the distant chair on the far right passes beyond the right image boundary. The map usefully combines the central chair and its two pillows into one coherent object region and distinguishes both the small windowsill plant and the distant chair despite the complicated illumination, but its category assignments and frame-to-frame consistency are extremely unreliable. In particular, it wrongly calls the central and distant armchairs ‘couch’ or ‘bed,’ identifies the phone as ‘chair’/‘remote’ in frame 4, entirely omits the person’s upper head at the top right, removes their body mask completely in frames 3 and 5, and falsely detects a ‘potted plant’ on the decorative box sitting on the low left table, approximately 1.8 m away, in frame 3.
pose: Nearly all of the pose visualization is empty throughout the five frames. Its sole detection is a tiny yellow 2D body skeleton in the lower-left quadrant of frame 2, positioned where the smartphone screen appears about 0.6 m from the camera wearer; no magenta hand skeletons are detected anywhere. That lone pose belongs to a miniature full-body person shown on the phone screen held by the individual on the right. On the display, the figure stands upright and faces forward or slightly right, whereas the real person seated roughly 0.4–0.7 m to the camera wearer’s right is not represented at all. The egocentric framing cuts off most of the actual person along the bottom and right boundaries, leaving only their nose and chin in profile near the top right, a narrow portion of patterned shirt in the lower right, and both hands gripping the phone at the bottom. Consequently, the pose model detects none of their torso, head, or hands in any of the 5 frames. Although frame 2’s pose map draws attention to a human figure on the dimly illuminated phone screen that is minute and difficult to spot quickly in the RGB view, it provides entirely unreliable scene-level spatial information because it misses both the nearby individual and their within-reach hands for the full sequence.
